questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what a blank cheque committed a state to
questions.stem: In 1914 Austria-Hungary promised Germany support if war came, and Germany then told Austria it would stand by her whatever she decided. What did that second promise actually commit Germany to?

options.text: An unconditional obligation, so a quarrel in the Balkans could pull Germany into war

options.misconception: reverses an unconditional pledge into a conditional parliamentary one
options.text: A promise to send troops only after a German cabinet had voted for them

options.misconception: invents an Italian defection clause no such treaty contained
options.text: An agreement to keep fighting even if Austria refused to negotiate first

options.misconception: invents a transfer of alliance the German pledge never provided
options.text: A treaty handing the whole alliance over to Italy within one year

questions.explanation: Whatever she decided removed the step where Germany would weigh the case, so the local crisis between Austria and Serbia became a German commitment as well. The tempting answers soften the pledge into a cabinet vote, invent an Italian clause, or invent a treaty over the whole alliance, none of which the promise itself contained.
questions.hint: What did the word whatever removed from the decision?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the case a wartime memorandum makes
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1914 navy memorandum argues that a later start would leave new battleships unbuilt, that gunnery practice would fall behind, and that the fleet would one day meet a rival's ships already at sea. What case is the memorandum making?

options.text: Delay is itself a cost, since building ships and training crews take years that cannot be recalled

options.misconception: inverts a memorandum written to justify acting before a rival does
options.text: The fleet must wait for a stronger ally before any new ship is laid down

options.misconception: argues the opposite of a document written to justify building
options.text: Naval building should stop, since land armies decide European wars anyway

options.misconception: reverses the timing, since waiting is what widens the gap
options.text: Ships should be finished only after a foreign war has already begun

questions.explanation: The memorandum counts years, not battles: hulls need slipways, guns need practice, and crews need time, so a decision to wait hands a permanent lead to a rival that is not obliged to wait too. The tempting answers invert the timing into a pause for allies, or stop the building the document exists to justify.
questions.hint: What kind of thing does the memorandum say cannot be hurried?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how a rivalry becomes a cause of war
questions.stem: Before 1914 two governments' newspapers accused each other of stealing frontiers, and both parliaments voted money for larger fleets. What made that rivalry a cause of war rather than mere talk?

options.text: The rivalry hardened into armaments, so claims about borders now had guns and budgets behind them

options.misconception: invents a standing pact that no power would ever sign
options.text: Both governments had signed a treaty requiring them to go to war within ten years

options.misconception: rules out the real basis, which was armed competition
options.text: The accusations were untrue, so the whole dispute rested on rumor and paper

options.misconception: claims censorship ended a rivalry that grew for years
options.text: Closing the foreign presses in 1911 stopped the rivalry where it began

questions.explanation: Talk becomes a cause when money turns it into hardware: once both sides have spent years on fleets and voted budgets, backing down means admitting the other outbuilt you, and the stakes stop being words. The tempting answers require a secret war pact, or drain the dispute of the arms race the money votes prove.
questions.hint: What did a vote for a larger fleet change about the argument?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a local war became general
questions.learningObjective: explain the chain that widened a regional war
questions.stem: When Austria moved against Serbia in July 1914, Russia's mobilization set German plans in motion and France's backing for Russia brought in a further power. What made the war general?

options.text: Mutual defense pledges turned a local war into a chain of automatic interventions

options.misconception: confuses alliance treaties with a general rule of international law
options.text: One declaration of war legally compelled every other state to join the same side

options.misconception: invents a joint colonial administration between warring powers
options.text: Colonial empires were run as one administration, so empires fought as one bloc

options.misconception: invents a neutral vote that neutral states refused to take
options.text: Neutral states voted unanimously to join the side that was losing ground

questions.explanation: Each power had promised to move when a partner was attacked, and mobilization was the promise being kept, so the chain advanced because no state could stop it once started. The tempting answers replace treaties with a universal rule of law, invent a joint colonial administration, or claim neutrals voted themselves into the war.
questions.hint: Did each state choose afresh, or act on a standing promise?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: choose the step that lowers the risk of general war
questions.stem: In the last week of July 1914 a foreign minister has three levers: an ultimatum, mobilization, and a proposal for talks. Which choice most reduces the chance of general war?

options.text: Send the talks proposal and slow mobilization, letting a third party broker the dispute

options.misconception: converts a deadline into a trigger the other side must accept
options.text: Issue the ultimatum with a short deadline, since hesitation invites worse terms

options.misconception: treats a mobilization as a signal when it is a commitment
options.text: Mobilize at once, since a show of force will frighten the others into retreat

options.misconception: abandons the one move that keeps a path to agreement open
options.text: Withdraw the ambassador and close the border, avoiding any binding commitment

questions.explanation: Talks plus slow mobilization is the only pair that keeps the dispute arguable: the other side can still negotiate without conceding a fait accompli, and a third party has something to broker. The tempting answers convert a deadline into a trigger, treat mobilization as a signal when it is a promise to fight, or close the channel that the crisis still needed.
questions.hint: Which lever can be used without spending it?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: read two series against each other rather than in isolation
questions.stem: Two navy tables are placed side by side: one power's battleship tonnage stays near four hundred thousand tons for a decade, while the other's climbs from three hundred thousand to past a million by 1913. What does that gap show?

options.text: One state put money into the sea instead of the land, and the other kept a balanced fleet

options.misconception: reads a widening gap as though the two totals had converged
options.text: Both fleets grew alike, so neither held a clear lead by the end of the period

options.misconception: invents a price comparison the tonnage tables do not give
options.text: The smaller fleet cost less per ton because its ships carried heavier guns

options.misconception: reverses the relation between new construction and weight
options.text: The larger total shows an older fleet, since newer hulls always weigh less

questions.explanation: A flat series beside a tripling one is a choice of priorities, not a difference of effort: one government held its fleet steady and put its money elsewhere while the other let the sea absorb its budget. The tempting answers call a widening gap convergence, and add price and age comparisons that a table of tonnage cannot supply.
questions.hint: One line is flat and one is not. What does a flat line mean?

questions.topic: Why the United States entered the war
questions.learningObjective: link two separate events to a decision to intervene
questions.stem: In 1917 American troops landed after unrestricted submarine warfare resumed and after a German agent's offer of alliance to Mexico was made public. What linked those events to American entry?

options.misconception: reverses a proposed alliance into a Mexican defeat
options.text: Mexico had already joined Germany, so the United States entered to defend Mexico

options.misconception: misreads neutral trading rules as a shipbuilding contract
options.text: American industry had been hired to build German warships as the war began

options.misconception: invents a neutrality pledge the declaration of war contradicts
options.text: The United States had pledged neutrality in writing and withdrew the pledge

questions.explanation: A sinking of neutral ships with American dead made the question of restraint impossible to answer politically, and the telegram offered by Germany removed the last story that the war was somebody else's doing. questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the consequence of a defeated ally's exit
questions.stem: Russia's government collapsed in 1917, the new leaders refused to continue the war, and in 1918 the Central Powers took large Russian territories. Why did that sequence matter to the whole war?

options.text: Russia's exit freed German divisions for the west and hastened the final defeat

options.misconception: reverses the freed troops, which passed to the German side
options.text: Russia's exit added trained German soldiers to the western Allies at once

options.misconception: puts immediate peace at the door of a treaty signed two years later
options.text: Russia's exit forced Germany to accept peace terms within a few weeks

options.misconception: calls an end to a campaign that continued through 1918
options.text: Russia's exit ended the war at once, with no further fighting in 1918

questions.explanation: An army of millions on the eastern front could now be moved west, and a state that had spent years refusing a separate peace finally had one, so the balance of the war shifted sharply in 1918. The tempting answers send the freed troops to the other side, or compress into weeks or days a collapse that took the best part of a year to finish.
questions.hint: Where could a million soldiers suddenly be sent, and to whom?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a war plan that counted on time failed
questions.stem: German admirals welcomed American neutrality in 1916 and planned to sink merchant ships fast enough to starve Britain before the United States could build ships to replace them. Explain why the plan failed.

options.text: Sinkings ran ahead of the estimate, so American yards launched more tonnage and opinion turned

options.misconception: invents a single-month loss of the submarine fleet
options.text: The British navy found and sank the whole submarine force within one month

options.misconception: contradicts the shipbuilding the plan counted on to fail
options.text: American shipyards refused to build cargo vessels for any foreign flag at all

options.misconception: confuses German food with British, which the blockade targeted
options.text: The plan was abandoned because German food stocks were plentiful by 1916

questions.explanation: The plan assumed a rate of sinking slow enough to outrun American shipbuilding, and the actual rate was faster, so each sunk ship bought a few weeks of argument and a new hull bought a few weeks of supply, until the losses and the headlines together ended American neutrality. The tempting answers invent a lost submarine fleet, a refusal to build ships, or plentiful German food, none of which the campaign's record shows.
questions.hint: Which of the two rates did the plan assume wrongly?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: compare how the two wars began
questions.stem: Two original summaries compare the openings of the two wars: one says 1914 grew from pledges, blunders, and calculations that ran past anyone's control, the other says 1939 grew from a settled plan to reverse a lost war. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: Both followed failed diplomacy, but in 1939 the leaders knew the cost and chose the war anyway

options.misconception: erases the difference between a slip and a settled plan
options.text: The two are alike, since one deliberate plan produced both wars in the same way

options.misconception: reduces 1914 to one event and 1939 to none at all
options.text: Only 1914 was a real war, since 1939 was settled by a single assassination alone

options.misconception: ignores the crises both summaries put at the start
options.text: Neither opening involved a diplomatic crisis, since both began with an invasion

questions.explanation: Both openings begin in failed diplomacy, but the difference the summaries isolate is who was in control: in 1914 commitments outran judgment, while in 1939 a government that remembered the cost of the last war judged the same failure worth another. The tempting answers flatten that difference, or move the deliberate cause into the accidental war and none into the deliberate one.
questions.hint: What does the word plan mean that the first summary lacks?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain why the state began directing industry
questions.stem: In 1915 a British ministry began fixing the price of shells, ordering steel by the ton, and building state factories where private firms had missed delivery dates. What did that reveal about the war economy?

options.text: The state had to plan, price, and build what private industry would not deliver in time

options.misconception: turns state direction of supply into completed national ownership
options.text: Private industry was nationalized outright and its owners were paid nothing

options.misconception: confuses a power to set prices with a cut in order sizes
options.text: The government cured the shell shortage by ordering fewer and smaller shells

options.misconception: ignores the output that kept rising after 1915
options.text: Arms production was judged unnecessary once the war settled into trenches

questions.explanation: Contracts alone could not deliver millions of shells on a political timetable, so the state set a price, took over ordering, and built capacity itself, which is the moment wartime demand outruns the market. The tempting answers convert direction into nationalization, shrink the order book, or declare production unnecessary at the very moment output was rising.
questions.hint: Why does a price the government fixes make delivery worth guaranteeing?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: judge what a pair of statistics actually licenses
questions.stem: Between 1914 and 1918 one country's share of women in industrial employment doubles, and total output rises over the same years. Which conclusion does that pair of figures actually support?

options.text: That more women worked in industry and the economy expanded, but not that the war caused either

options.misconception: denies the doubling the figures plainly record
options.text: That women had always worked in industry, so the war changed nothing in the figures

options.misconception: assigns sole causation to a change the figures cannot isolate
options.text: That rising output was caused entirely by the increase in women's employment

options.misconception: claims a total displacement the totals themselves do not support
options.text: That women's work pushed every man out of the labor market by the end of the war

questions.explanation: Two series moving together in the same years show that both happened and nothing about which caused which, since a third factor, orders and mobilization, moved with them. questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a blockade was meant to work
questions.learningObjective: state the mechanism a blockade relied on
questions.stem: Britain declared a blockade of the German coast in 1914 and enforced it over a wide sea area, stopping ships that entered. How was that weapon meant to work?

options.text: By cutting off food and raw material reaching the enemy and waiting out a short war

options.misconception: confuses a naval blockade with an amphibious landing
options.text: By landing troops on the German coast within weeks of the declaration

options.misconception: claims a diplomatic effect neutral states refused at first
options.text: By forcing every neutral state into the war against Germany at once

options.misconception: compresses years of substitution into a single season
options.text: By replacing German coal and steel in world markets within one season

questions.explanation: A blockade is a wager on time: imports shrink, substitutes and rationing follow, and a government facing hunger and short fuel reaches a settlement, provided the war does not last long enough for growers and firms to adapt. The tempting answers turn it into an invasion, a diplomatic landslide, or a single-season industrial miracle.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what state control of prices achieved
questions.stem: One government created ministries for supply, aircraft, and food, and issued ration books fixing what each household might buy at what price. What did that machinery achieve?

options.text: It passed scarce goods by need rather than by price, so the queue replaced the market

options.misconception: reverses rationing into its abolition inside a single war
options.text: It ended rationing by reopening ordinary shops to private trade within weeks

options.misconception: confuses wartime direction of output with full national ownership
options.text: It removed private firms from manufacturing and put every plant under the state

options.misconception: confuses setting prices with a free market the war suspended
options.text: It left the market to decide, merely recording prices after they had been set

questions.explanation: When supply is short, a price that clears the market sends the goods to whoever pays most, so fixing allocations and prices is how a state decides to share the shortage by household instead. The tempting answers abolish the rationing, nationalize industry wholesale, or describe bookkeeping over a market the war had already suspended.
questions.hint: If there is not enough for everyone, what decides who gets it?

questions.topic: An order reaching the shop counter
questions.learningObjective: identify the reach of wartime administration in one document
questions.stem: An original summary of a wartime order tells shopkeepers to record every sale of fuel and food, forbids sale without a coupon, and sets penalties for sellers who break the rule. What does such an order show?

options.text: The state reached into ordinary shops to enforce its own ration rules in person

options.misconception: confuses inspection and records with nationalization of retail
options.text: The government had taken over every shop and appointed all of the sales clerks

options.misconception: mistakes enforceable rules for a promise with no penalty
options.text: Rationing existed only as an informal promise that shopkeepers would keep

options.misconception: reverses scarcity, since rules of this kind exist because supply was short
options.text: Food was plentiful that year and the rules existed only to raise prices

questions.explanation: A coupon, a record book, and a penalty is the state writing its rules into the daily transaction, which is what total war means: administration ends at the shop door rather than at the ministry. The tempting answers turn inspection into nationalization, enforcement into a promise, and shortage into abundance.
questions.hint: Where does the rule in that order actually get obeyed?

options.text: That Britain had too few crews to man the fleet and had to leave ships idle

options.misconception: confuses civilian volunteers with a professional-only navy
options.text: That only professional sailors could be trusted to take a fighting vessel out

options.misconception: invents a secret agreement to arm enemy raiders

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain how borrowing became a weapon of state
questions.stem: In 1917 a state issued bonds to its own citizens, which its finance minister praised, and went on buying material it could not yet pay for. Explain why credit settled so much of the war.

options.text: Credit lets a state pledge future taxes for present goods, so control of credit became control of supply

options.misconception: confuses a promise to repay with printing money that devalues it
options.text: Credit simply raised prices, so any state with paper money could buy whatever it liked

options.misconception: narrows credit to wages and ignores contracts for materials
options.text: Credit mattered only for paying soldiers, since goods were never bought on account

options.misconception: ranks credit above production though both were needed to fight
options.text: Credit settled the arguments between states, so material strength hardly mattered

options.text: Food was plentiful, so the advice was a campaign against waste in peacetime alone

options.misconception: converts a request for thrift into a draft for farm workers
options.text: Farm labor conscripts had to report daily to the ministry for their assignments

options.misconception: encourages the very gardening the pamphlet is asking readers to take up
options.text: Private gardens were declared illegal, so only state allotments could grow food

questions.explanation: When a government asks its citizens to mend, grow, and save, it has run out of official levers and is recruiting the household as an unpaid supply corps, which is the home front's own contribution to the war. The tempting answers read abundance into scarcity, invent a labor draft, and outlaw the gardening the pamphlet actually promotes.
questions.hint: Why ask a household to mend a coat if new ones are arriving?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shape of the peace settlement
questions.learningObjective: classify a settlement from the clauses it imposes
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1919 settlement records fixed land losses, an occupying army, a sum in money, and an article naming every government official who must be tried. What kind of settlement is described?

options.text: A punitive one, written to weaken the defeated state and keep it under watch

options.misconception: describes the opposite intent of clauses made to restrict the loser
options.text: A lenient one, written so the defeated state could keep most of its strength

options.misconception: misreads a political settlement as a commercial one
options.text: A trading agreement, since the clauses concern tariffs and merchants' rights

options.misconception: confuses restrictions on a loser with mutual defense among allies
options.text: An alliance treaty, since every power guaranteed the others' borders in writing

questions.explanation: Territory, money, a garrison, and personal liability are the four things a victor imposes when it wants the loser weakened, occupied, and never again able to start the war alone, and the victors expected the terms to make peace rather than provoke revenge. The tempting answers reverse the intent, or relabel a political judgment as tariffs or a mutual guarantee.
questions.hint: Who pays, and who is judged, in these clauses?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a council could not stop a war
questions.learningObjective: explain the weakness of a recommendation-only body
questions.stem: A league at Geneva required a state facing war to bring its complaint to a council, and the council could only recommend what members should do. Why was that arrangement weak?

options.text: Recommending is not compelling, so a great power could simply ignore the whole process

options.misconception: reverses the council's composition, which included small states too
options.text: No small state had a seat, so only the weakest members were ever heard

options.misconception: mistakes the place of meeting for the reason it could not act
options.text: The chosen city was too far away for members to assemble in good time

options.misconception: confuses a budget detail with the power the body lacked
options.text: The league had no money at all, not even enough to pay its own clerks

questions.explanation: A body that can only recommend has no way to make a great power obey, and the states most likely to break the peace are the ones least able to be impressed by a vote in a hall, so the arrangement assumed cooperation from exactly the governments least inclined to give it. The tempting answers blame the seats, the venue, or an empty treasury, none of which the power to act depends on.
questions.hint: What is the difference between a recommendation and an order?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what mandates let victors claim without annexing
questions.stem: Treaties named former territories and told the winning powers to govern them until they could stand alone, with the reports published. Why did the victors choose that wording?

options.text: To claim rule without annexing, so each power took territory without inviting criticism

options.misconception: inverts a promise of eventual self-rule into immediate independence
options.text: To promise self-government at once, so that no power would rule those lands at all

options.misconception: invents elections the mandate system replaced with appointed rulers
options.text: To hand the territories to local assemblies elected by their inhabitants

options.misconception: ignores that the system was made for non-European subjects
options.text: To reserve the territories for a future empire made up only of Europeans

questions.explanation: Annexing a non-European territory invited the charge of conquest that the war had been fought to end, so a mandate let a victor govern in a borrowed name, with a promise and a published report to prove it meant to leave. The tempting answers invert the promise, invent elections the system avoided, or turn a compromise about non-European subjects into a European empire.
questions.hint: What was the wording a victor needed in order to hold the land?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Debts and reparations side by side
questions.learningObjective: compare two financial scales rather than one in isolation
questions.stem: A 1920s table sets one country's reparations at about two billion gold marks a year, while British and French war debts to the United States together exceed four billion a year, and an economist argued both sums were beyond paying. What does the table show?

options.text: Debts and reparations together were large enough to strain every budget involved

options.misconception: reverses two totals the table lists side by side
options.text: Reparations were larger than the British and French debts added together

options.misconception: adds a figure the table does not contain to excuse the payments
options.text: The sums were small next to that country's income from overseas investments

options.misconception: claims a nil payment the table's own schedule contradicts
options.text: Reparations were never actually paid in any year after 1921

questions.explanation: Two large transfers crossing borders in the same years, one from a defeated state and one from victors to a creditor, are what a table like this exposes: money owed is money that has to come out of someone's budget, and two such claims at once are harder than either alone. The tempting answers reverse the totals, add an income figure the table lacks, or deny payments the schedule itself records.
questions.hint: Which of the two figures is larger, and does that settle the question?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the settlement fed the crash
questions.learningObjective: weigh two accounts of the same economic collapse
questions.stem: Two original summaries link the 1930s: one traces the collapse of trade, banks, and work to debts owed after the war, the other ties it to nations bound together by reparations and by the loans taken out to pay them. Which synthesis fits?

options.text: Debts and reparations moved money between countries, so one country's crisis became everyone's

options.misconception: denies the cross-border money the second summary traces
options.text: The collapse had a single local cause, since no money crossed any border after 1919

options.misconception: ignores trade and credit that both summaries name
options.text: Trade and credit were irrelevant, since the crisis began in the countryside alone

options.misconception: reduces a debt crisis to a shortage of coinage
options.text: The crisis came from a shortage of coins, since reparations were paid entirely in cash

questions.explanation: The second summary explains the reach the first cannot: a collapse traced to debt becomes continental because the same settlement made governments, banks, and investors across Europe owe and be owed each other, so one default passes down a chain of credits. The tempting answers localize a crisis the loans connect, drop trade and credit from the account, or reduce it to a shortage of coin.
questions.hint: Why would a banking crisis in one country shut factories in another?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain the selective use of self-determination
questions.stem: A victorious power in 1945 spoke of peoples deciding their own future, yet kept several territories and peoples outside that promise. Explain why the principle was applied unevenly.

options.text: The promise was strong where old European claims mattered and weak where a rival held the land

options.misconception: calls political choice an error where calculations were made
options.text: The promise was strong everywhere and every exception was simply a mistake

options.misconception: confuses self-determination with membership in the winning alliance
options.text: The principle applied only to peoples who had fought on the winning side

options.misconception: invents a colonial vote that no settlement provided
options.text: The promise was withdrawn in 1945 because subject peoples voted to keep it

questions.explanation: The same principle redrew Europe, where old claims overlapped and the victors cared, and left empire intact where a rival's forces or investments stood in the way, so the inconsistency was a matter of interest rather than of principle. The tempting answers call that inconsistency a blunder, restrict the principle to allies, or invent a colonial vote that no settlement ever held.
questions.hint: Where were rival armies still standing when the promises were made?
